title: Simulacro 08 — Consenso, leader election y coordinación distribuida
focus: Raft y Paxos, leader election, split-brain, quorums, Zookeeper vs etcd vs Consul, distributed locks (por qué son peligrosos), fencing tokens y por qué el consenso siempre paga latencia.

questions.scenario: Un colega jr dice: '¿por qué necesitamos Raft si podemos hacer un algoritmo simple de vote-and-majority?'. Otro senior menciona 'FLP' y el jr se queda perdido.
questions.question: ¿Qué es el teorema FLP y qué implica para el consenso distribuido?

options.text: FLP (Fischer-Lynch-Paterson 1985) prueba que en un sistema asíncrono con AL MENOS UN nodo fallando, NO existe algoritmo determinista que resuelva consenso en tiempo acotado. Implicación: cualquier protocolo de consenso real (Paxos, Raft) debe usar timeouts (asumiendo parcial sincronía) o randomness — jamás garantiza terminación en asincronía pura.
options.why: Correcto. FLP es uno de los resultados MÁS importantes de la teoría distribuida. En modelo asíncrono puro (sin bounds en delay de mensajes/procesamiento), incluso un único fallo puede prevenir consenso indefinidamente. Todos los algoritmos prácticos (Paxos, Raft, Zab) escapan asumiendo 'partial synchrony' (Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer 1988) — timeouts eventuales bounded — o usan randomization (Ben-Or). Es por eso que Raft/Paxos tienen leader lease timeouts y election timeouts.

options.text: FLP prueba que el consenso es imposible.
options.why: Simplificación errónea. FLP dice consenso deterministic garantizado imposible en asincronía pura. En práctica, con timeouts asumiendo eventual delivery, consenso es alcanzable. FLP explica POR QUÉ Raft usa timeouts, no que Raft no funcione.

options.text: FLP es el teorema CAP renombrado.
options.why: Son teoremas distintos: CAP (Brewer 2000, Gilbert-Lynch 2002) trata sobre availability vs consistency ante particiones. FLP (1985) es más fundamental: incluso sin particiones, en modelo asíncrono puro consenso deterministic garantizado es imposible con 1 fallo.

options.text: FLP aplica solo a Byzantine failures.
options.why: Falso. FLP aplica al modelo más simple: crash failures (nodos se caen sin comportamiento malicioso). Byzantine consensus es aún más difícil (Lamport-Shostak-Pease 1982, PBFT). FLP asume el caso benigno y aún así prueba impossibility en asincronía pura.

questions.explanation: FLP (1985) marca un antes y después en teoría distribuida. Modelo: N procesos, comunicación async (mensajes eventualmente entregados, sin bound), 1 puede crash. Consenso: acordar UN valor entre los proposed. Teorema: no existe algoritmo deterministic que siempre termine. Intuition: 'crashed' vs 'muy lento' son indistinguibles en async — no puedes safely proceder sin risking violate agreement. Solución práctica: (1) Asumir partial synchrony (DLS 1988) — mensajes se entregan en bound eventual conocido. Timeouts implementan esto. Paxos, Raft, PBFT lo asumen. (2) Randomization — Ben-Or algorithms terminan con probability 1 sin timeouts. Usado en algunos Byzantine consensus (HoneyBadger). Consecuencias prácticas: (a) Todo consensus protocol tiene timeouts que pueden causar spurious leader elections. (b) Under network chaos, consenso puede stall. (c) 'Eventual consistency' es en parte una respuesta a FLP: si consenso es tan caro, evita necesitarlo cuando puedas.
questions.realWorld: Todos los sistemas basados en Raft (etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, RethinkDB, TiKV) tienen 'election timeout' precisely por FLP. Zookeeper Zab lo mismo. Bug famoso: etcd bajo network chaos podía tener leader elections repetidas indefinidas (bug fix con Pre-Vote optimization de Raft, 2015). Ver 'Diego Ongaro's Raft thesis' donde discute FLP explícitamente.

references.title: Fischer, Lynch, Paterson — 'Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process', JACM 1985
Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer — 'Consensus in the presence of partial synchrony', JACM 1988

questions.scenario: Debate técnico: '¿por qué Raft en vez de Paxos, si Paxos es más antiguo y probado?'
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la razón principal del auge de Raft en 2014+?

options.text: Raft es más rápido matemáticamente.
options.why: Falso — asymptotically son equivalentes (O(1) rounds para consenso normal en buen caso). Raft no gana en performance; gana en OTRA cosa.

options.text: Raft (Ongaro-Ousterhout 2014) fue diseñado explícitamente para UNDERSTANDABILITY. Paxos (Lamport 1998) es notoriamente difícil de entender — 'Paxos Made Simple' sigue siendo difícil. Raft descompone en 3 subproblemas claros (leader election, log replication, safety), tiene un leader fuerte, y estructura ordenada del log. Como resultado, Raft se ha implementado correctamente decenas de veces (etcd, Consul, TiKV, CockroachDB, RethinkDB, ScyllaDB) mientras Paxos production correcto solo lo tienen Google (Chubby, Spanner) y pocos más.
options.why: Correcto. El paper de Raft literalmente se llama 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm'. Ongaro-Ousterhout hicieron user study demostrando students entienden Raft mejor que Paxos. Consecuencia industrial: correctness improved (Paxos implementations históricamente tienen bugs sutiles), adopción explota. Raft no es 'better' teóricamente; es implementable correctamente. Como Ongaro dice: 'the primary goal of Raft is teachability, correctness follows'.

options.text: Raft es más eficiente en uso de bandwidth.
options.why: Falso — Raft y Paxos tienen complexity similar. Raft en algunos casos es LESS eficiente (leader-based, single leader es bottleneck; Multi-Paxos también, EPaxos elimina leader). Ganancia no es eficiencia.

options.text: Raft soporta Byzantine failures.
options.why: Falso. Raft (como Paxos clásico) asume crash-only failures. Byzantine tolerance requiere PBFT o similares (Tendermint, HotStuff).

questions.explanation: Historia: Lamport publicó 'The Part-Time Parliament' (1998) describiendo Paxos con analogía histórica que confundió a todos. 'Paxos Made Simple' (2001) intentó clarificar pero sigue siendo difícil. En década 2000s, Google Chubby usó Paxos internamente pero paper aclaraba complexity de implementarlo correctly. Diego Ongaro (Stanford) diseñó Raft para tesis PhD (2014) con OBJETIVO explícito de understandability. Publicó paper 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm' y open-source implementation. Etcd (CoreOS) adoptó Raft, luego Kubernetes usa etcd → adopción explota. Consul, TiKV, CockroachDB, muchos más. Raft properties: (1) Strong leader — solo leader accepts writes, simplifies. (2) Log matching — leader replicates log entries, followers copy. (3) Leader election — randomized timeouts prevent split votes. (4) Safety — Election Restriction (leader must have all committed entries) + Log Matching. Verificación formal: Raft ha sido model-checked (TLA+ specs) más que Paxos. La lección meta: DESIGN FOR UNDERSTANDABILITY es una decision ingenieril válida en sistemas críticos.
questions.realWorld: Etcd (Kubernetes control plane store) es Raft. Consul (HashiCorp) es Raft. TiKV / TiDB, YugabyteDB, CockroachDB usan Raft con multi-Raft (una instance de Raft por range/partition). Redis Sentinel usa Raft-like para failover. Google Chubby usa Paxos (histórico). Spanner usa Paxos por Paxos group per range. Kafka usa KRaft (Kafka Raft) desde 2.8, reemplazando Zookeeper (que usa Zab, Raft-like).

references.title: Ongaro, Ousterhout — 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm', ATC 2014

questions.scenario: Cluster de 3 nodos Raft. Network partition aísla al leader (nodo A) de los otros dos (B, C). B y C eligen a B como nuevo leader. A no sabe que perdió — sigue aceptando writes de clientes que aún pueden alcanzarlo.
questions.question: ¿Cómo previene Raft split-brain en este escenario?

options.text: Raft requiere MAYORÍA (quorum > N/2) para aceptar writes. Con N=3, quorum=2. Después de partición, A tiene solo 1 nodo (él mismo) — no puede committear nada (no alcanza quorum). B (con C) alcanza quorum=2 → puede committear. Los writes de A NO se comprometen (writes propuestos, no ack'd → cliente ve timeout/error). Además, Raft usa 'term numbers': cuando A ve un term mayor (del new leader), se convierte en follower automáticamente.
options.why: Correcto. La combinación de: (1) mayoría estricta para commit (impide dos leaders con quorum simultáneamente en partition), (2) term numbers monotónicos (leader más nuevo gana), (3) log matching + election restriction (leader nuevo debe tener todos los committed entries), previene split-brain SAFETY (no committed writes divergentes). AVAILABILITY se pierde en la partición minoritaria (nadie sirve writes), pero safety se preserva.

options.text: Raft usa timestamps para determinar qué write es el 'real'.
options.why: Confusión con LWW. Raft no usa wall-clock timestamps. Usa term numbers (monotonic counter incrementado en cada election) + log index. Wall-clock es unreliable en distributed — Raft evita depender de él para safety.

options.text: Raft acepta ambos leaders temporalmente y luego reconcilia por votación.
options.why: Anti-thesis de Raft. NUNCA hay dos leaders con quorum simultáneamente (safety property). El leader viejo puede creerse leader pero no puede committear (necesita quorum). Cuando la partición sana, aprende del term mayor y step down.

options.text: Depende de la configuración de STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head).
options.why: STONITH es técnica de HA clustering (Pacemaker, DRBD) — fence node caído con power off. Es un mecanismo externo, no de Raft. Raft resuelve safety con quorum sin necesitar STONITH.

questions.explanation: Raft safety properties (proved formalmente): (1) Election Safety — solo un leader per term. (2) Leader Append-Only — leader never overwrites/deletes entries. (3) Log Matching — same index+term = same content en todos los logs. (4) Leader Completeness — leader tiene todos los committed entries de terms anteriores. (5) State Machine Safety — todos apply same entries en same order. Estas dan safety incluso bajo partitions, delays, message reordering. Mechanism: (a) Term números monotónicos globales — cada leader election increments term. Higher term wins. (b) Election requiere quorum votes. (c) Vote grant condition: candidate log must be 'at least as up-to-date' as voter's (compares last log term, then index). (d) Commit rule: leader waits for majority replicated before considering entry committed. Bajo partición, minoritaria queda unavailable (no quorum) — sacrifice availability preserve safety (CP en CAP terms). Cuando partición sana, minority followers catch up del nuevo leader, discarding uncommitted entries divergentes.
questions.realWorld: Etcd durante network chaos: minority partition va read-only (o unavailable). Kubernetes control plane bloquea si etcd no tiene quorum. GitHub tuvo incidente 2018 donde MySQL Orchestrator (usaba Raft) tuvo split-brain no por bug de Raft sino por config incorrecta (fencing token mismatch). Consul, etcd, CockroachDB han sobrevivido Jepsen tests thanks to correct Raft implementation. Sistemas non-consensus (multi-master MySQL async) pueden crear split-brain silencioso porque no tienen quorum requirement.

references.title: Ongaro's Raft thesis — 'Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice', 2014

questions.scenario: Necesitas tolerancia a F fallos simultáneos en tu cluster de consenso. ¿Cuántos nodos requieres?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la fórmula correcta y por qué?

options.text: N = 2F + 1 (para crash faults). Ejemplos: tolerar 1 fallo = 3 nodos (quorum=2). Tolerar 2 fallos = 5 nodos (quorum=3). Tolerar 3 = 7 (quorum=4). Byzantine tolerance requiere N = 3F+1.
options.why: Correcto. Para crash fault tolerance (nodos caen benignamente): N=2F+1 permite tolerar F fallos manteniendo quorum. Con N=3 y 1 caído, quorum=2 (los 2 restantes) puede seguir. Con N=5 y 2 caídos, quorum=3 (3 restantes) puede seguir. Byzantine fault tolerance (nodos maliciosos/faulty aleatoriamente) es más difícil: N=3F+1 (Lamport 1982). Con Byzantine también requiere signed messages para eficiencia (PBFT).

options.text: N = F para tolerar F fallos.
options.why: Incorrecto: con N=F, si F caen, quedan 0 — no puede haber quorum. Necesitas más para retener mayoría tras fallos.
Insuficiente para consenso. Con N=F+1 y F caídos, queda 1 — no puede formar quorum (por definición >N/2 = > (F+1)/2, con F=1: quorum > 1 = 2, pero solo queda 1). Necesitas al menos N=2F+1.

options.text: Depende del algoritmo (Paxos vs Raft difieren).
options.why: Falso: Paxos y Raft usan mismas fórmulas (mayoría estricta). La diferencia es en cómo COORDINAN, no en cuánto tolerantcia. Byzantine algorithms difieren (PBFT es 3F+1).

questions.explanation: Deriva simple: quorum debe ser > N/2 (mayoría estricta). Para que después de F fallos siga habiendo quorum: N - F > N/2 → N > 2F → N ≥ 2F+1. Configuraciones comunes: 3 nodos (tolera 1), 5 nodos (tolera 2), 7 nodos (tolera 3). Rara vez más — cost/benefit deteriora. 5 es sweet spot típico. Byzantine: PBFT requires 3F+1 porque nodos maliciosos pueden mentir en votes. Con 3F+1 y F maliciosos, quorum de 2F+1 asegura majority honest. Consideraciones prácticas: (1) Availability zones — spread nodos across AZs to tolerate zone failure. Con N=5, 2 AZ (2+3 split) → losing one AZ leaves 3 (quorum!) OK; losing the other leaves 2, no quorum. Ideal 3 AZs with N=3 (1 per AZ) o N=5 (2+2+1). (2) Odd N — even N wastes tolerance (N=4 tolerates same as N=3, 1 fault). (3) Larger N = more latency (more nodes to ack). (4) Rara vez más de 7 — practical cost.
questions.realWorld: etcd deployments típicos: 3 nodos (dev/small clusters), 5 (production, tolera 2 caídos). Kubernetes recomienda 3 o 5 master nodes. CockroachDB usa 3 o 5 replicas per range across zones. ZooKeeper 3 o 5 nodos. Blockchain BFT protocols (Tendermint, Cosmos) usan N=3F+1 typically 100+ validators for practical Byzantine tolerance. AWS DynamoDB internal use 3-way replication with quorum. La regla 2F+1 es fundamental y aparece en todo consensus system.

questions.scenario: Nueva plataforma necesita coordination service: leader election, service discovery, config store, distributed locks. Debate entre Zookeeper, etcd, y Consul.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son las diferencias PRÁCTICAS y cuándo elegir cada uno?

options.text: ZooKeeper (Zab, Java) — más antiguo, batalla-probado (Hadoop, Kafka pre-KRaft, HBase). API zNodes hierarchical. Menos amigable de operar. etcd (Raft, Go) — moderno, focus en simplicity + reliability. gRPC API, Kubernetes lo usa como store. Consul (Raft, Go) — HashiCorp, incluye service discovery + health checks + DNS interface + KV. Más 'batteries included' para service mesh scenarios. Elegir por ecosystem: Hadoop/Kafka legacy → ZK; Kubernetes/cloud native → etcd; service discovery + mesh → Consul.
options.why: Correcto y matizado. Los tres proporcionan consensus (CP). Diferencias reales: (a) implementation language y ecosystem — Java historic infra vs Go cloud native. (b) API surface — ZK zNodes vs etcd KV con leases vs Consul KV + service catalog + health. (c) Feature scope — etcd minimalist, Consul incluye service mesh (Connect) + multi-DC. (d) Operability — etcd/Consul percibidos more operator-friendly (mejor tooling, docs, observability). Elección por use case dominant.

options.text: Los tres son intercambiables — elegir por gusto personal.
options.why: Simplifica. Tienen diferentes APIs, feature sets, ecosystems, operational characteristics. Migration entre ellos es no-trivial. Elección arquitectural con consecuencias multi-año.

options.text: Zookeeper siempre — es el más probado.
options.why: Válido para Hadoop-era workloads pero Kafka mismo migró a KRaft (removing Zookeeper dependency). Cloud native infra (Kubernetes, Docker Swarm) adopta etcd/Consul. 'Battle-tested' no equivale a 'mejor elección' en nuevos deployments.

options.text: Los usa siempre juntos: Zookeeper para coordinación + etcd para config + Consul para service discovery.
options.why: Overkill absurdo. Duplicar coordination infrastructure multiplica operational load y consistency issues (¿quién es fuente de verdad?). Elige UNO.

questions.explanation: Coordination services son piedra angular de infra distribuida — cualquier bug o inestabilidad puede tumbar decenas de sistemas dependientes. Comparación 2026: (1) ZooKeeper (Apache, ~2008): Zab consensus (Raft-like predecessor), Java (JVM overhead), hierarchical zNodes, watches, ephemeral nodes for session management. Ecosystem: Hadoop, HBase, Kafka legacy, Solr. Cons: Java ops, older tooling. (2) etcd (CoreOS, ~2013): Raft, Go, gRPC API, watches, leases (TTL keys). Ecosystem: Kubernetes control plane store, CoreDNS, Rook. Cons: KV solo, sin service catalog nativo. (3) Consul (HashiCorp, ~2014): Raft, Go, KV + service catalog + health checks + DNS + Consul Connect (service mesh). Multi-DC federation. Ecosystem: HashiCorp stack, Vault, Nomad. Cons: mayor superficie (más features = más operational overhead). (4) Kafka KRaft (2021+): removes Zookeeper dependency from Kafka. Alternativa emergiendo: FoundationDB, Nats JetStream para casos específicos. Elegir por: ecosystem que ya usas, feature necesarios, operational skills del team. No hay 'ganador' absoluto.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes ETCD failure = control plane down. GitHub uses Consul for service discovery. Netflix uses Eureka (client-side discovery, less consensus needed). Airbnb uses Zookeeper legacy + migrating. Kafka 3.x+ ships KRaft removing Zookeeper (mucho más simple deploy). Uber built its own (M3, has similar features).

questions.topic: Distributed locks — por qué son peligrosos
questions.scenario: Team quiere garantizar que solo UN worker procese cada tarea. Consideran Redis SETNX + expire, o Zookeeper ephemeral node, o etcd lease. Manager senior dice: 'los locks distribuidos son problemáticos'.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el problema fundamental de los distributed locks?

options.text: Solo hay bugs de implementación. Redlock es correcto si se configura bien.
options.why: Falso. Martin Kleppmann demostró en 2016 que Redlock (algoritmo canónico distributed lock con Redis) NO ES SAFE bajo GC pauses, network delays, or clock jumps. Los problemas son fundamentales, no bugs.

options.text: Problema fundamental: cualquier lock con TTL sufre de 'client pause' (GC, VM suspension, network partition). El cliente puede creer aún tener el lock cuando el TTL expiró y otro lo adquirió. Sin fencing tokens (número monotónico devuelto al adquirir, validado por el RECURSO destino), el lock viejo puede corromper el sistema. Aunque ZooKeeper/etcd exponen fencing tokens (revision/zxid), el recurso destino (DB, file, API externa) DEBE cooperar validándolo — muchos no lo soportan.
options.why: Correcto. Kleppmann publicó 'How to do distributed locking' (2016) analizando por qué Redlock (5 Redis masters con majority) NO es safe. Problemas: (1) GC pause > TTL: cliente pierde lock sin saberlo, otro adquiere; cuando cliente despierta, ambos actúan. (2) Clock jumps: NTP correction o VM host jumping timestamps → TTL comparisons incorrect. (3) Network delays: mensaje de release/acquire llegan out of order. Solución: fencing tokens — recurso destino compara token, rechaza operations con token menor. ZK ofrece zxid (transaction id monotonic), etcd ofrece revision. Pero recurso destino DEBE validar. Muchos NO lo soportan (S3, arbitrary APIs).

options.text: Solo Redis tiene el problema; ZooKeeper es safe automáticamente.
options.why: Falso. ZooKeeper también tiene el problema — la diferencia es que ZK provee zxid como fencing token EXPUESTO al cliente, mientras Redlock no lo hace. Pero SEGURIDAD requiere el resource destino usar el token — no gratis.

options.text: Distributed locks son safe si usas TTLs cortos.
options.why: TTLs cortos aumentan rate de expiración espúrea bajo variability — más problemas, no menos. Y no eliminan pause del cliente. Solución no está en tuning TTL, está en fencing tokens + resource cooperation.

questions.explanation: Distributed locks problema fundamental es que representan 'exclusion mutua' que en async distributed model es notoriamente difícil. Kleppmann vs Antirez (autor de Redis) debate público sobre Redlock (2016) fue seminal. Análisis: (1) Any lock with TTL has window: cliente pausa > TTL → other client adquires → both active simultaneously. (2) Sin fencing tokens, el sistema no puede detectar/rechazar el operation del cliente viejo. (3) Fencing tokens: monotonically increasing number per lock acquisition. Resource stores 'last seen token' — rejects operations with lower token. Ejemplos correct implementation: Google Chubby (2006) diseñó fencing tokens from day one. Zab/ZooKeeper exposes zxid. Etcd's revision. Kafka has 'leader epoch' fencing for the same reason. Alternativas: (1) Diseño idempotente — dos workers procesando misma task producen mismo resultado (mejor en muchos casos). (2) Ownership por partition — hash(task_id) % N determina worker; no lock needed. (3) Leader election vía consensus — a diferencia de lock, leader es acordado por quorum, con lease + fencing. La regla staff: preferir soluciones que EVITEN necesitar locks distribuidos.
questions.realWorld: Kleppmann's 2016 blog post 'How to do distributed locking' es lectura obligatoria. Sistemas production que usan distributed locks correctly SIEMPRE tienen fencing tokens + resource cooperation. Google Chubby (paper 2006, Burrows) es el reference implementation. Aphyr (Jepsen) ha destruido claims de correctness de muchos distributed lock services. Uber, Slack, etc. prefieren particionar work para evitar locks.

references.title: Martin Kleppmann — 'How to do distributed locking' (2016)
Burrows — 'The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems', OSDI 2006

questions.scenario: Sistema con leader-follower architecture. Leader sends heartbeats every 100ms. Followers assume leader dead if no heartbeat in 500ms → trigger election. Bug: bajo GC pause de 2s en leader, followers eligen new leader, luego old leader despierta y continúa 'leading' → split-brain writes.
questions.question: ¿Qué mecanismo resuelve el problema?

options.text: Leader lease: el leader tiene un lease TIME-BOUND, por ejemplo 10s. Debe renovarlo antes de expirar (heartbeat + renewal). Si el leader NO renueva antes del lease expire (porque GC pause), NO puede aceptar writes tras despertar — su lease expired, se convierte follower. Los followers pueden elegir nuevo leader tras lease expire (más grace period). Requiere clock accuracy (o clock skew bounds).
options.why: Correcto. Leader lease es el mechanism canónico para evitar split-brain incluso ante GC pauses o network partitions. Property: only holder of valid lease can write. Old leader que despierta después del lease expire checkeará y no committea (su lease is expired). Requires clock synchronization within bounds (usually loose, few seconds). Google Chubby, Spanner (TrueTime), Aurora, etcd usan variants of leader lease.

options.text: Aumentar el heartbeat timeout a 30s.
options.why: Mitiga probabilidad pero no elimina — 30s GC pause es posible bajo memory pressure severa. Además aumenta detection latency: si leader realmente muere, sistema tarda 30s en detectar. Trade-off pobre.

options.text: Confiar que GC pauses no ocurren en producción.
options.why: Ignorancia. GC pauses ocurren rutinariamente en Java (major GCs), Go (STW), etc. Ignorarlas ha causado innumerable outages. Además VM suspension (hypervisor moves, snapshots) causa same effect.

options.text: Eliminar el leader y usar leaderless (Dynamo-style).
options.why: Cambio arquitectural masivo. Leader-based tiene ventajas (simplicity, serialized ordering); leaderless tiene otras trade-offs (write conflicts). Cambiar por evitar un bug específico es sobrereacción. Leader lease resuelve el bug preservando arch.

questions.explanation: Leader lease mechanism: (1) Leader granted lease valid for duration T (e.g., 10s). (2) Leader must actively renew before T expires (heartbeat + renew request). (3) Leader can accept writes ONLY if lease not expired. (4) After lease expire without renewal, leader steps down; followers can elect new leader (con additional grace period para safety). (5) Old leader que wakes up post-expire checkeará su lease invalid → NO opera. Requirements: (a) Bounded clock skew — leader y quorum must agree on time within some bound. Typical assumption: sub-second skew (NTP). (b) Leader validates lease OP LOCAL comparando local clock vs lease expiry. Google Chubby uses lease with grace period. Spanner uses TrueTime for tighter guarantees. Ceph uses monitor leases. Kafka KRaft leader has fetch timeouts (similar concept). Etcd Raft has leader lease read-only optimization. Sin leader lease, systems dependen en heartbeat alone → vulnerable to pause > timeout scenarios.
questions.realWorld: Google Chubby paper (2006) explícitamente designa leases as protection against these scenarios. Cassandra Materialized Views tuvo bug histórico donde leader assumption sin lease correcto causó inconsistencies. Aurora Cluster uses leases + fencing tokens for master election. Ceph Monitor cluster uses leader lease. Sin este mechanism, GC pauses o VM suspensions han causado split-brain reales en muchos sistemas.

questions.scenario: Recurso compartido: S3 bucket que múltiples workers pueden write. Worker A adquiere 'lock' vía ZooKeeper y comienza upload. GC pausa 5s, ZK ephemeral node expira, worker B adquiere lock y comienza otro upload. Ambos escriben al mismo file en S3. Corruption.
questions.question: ¿Cómo resolvería fencing tokens este problema?

options.text: Cada adquisición de lock devuelve un TOKEN monotónicamente creciente (ej. ZK zxid, etcd revision, epoch number). Worker incluye el token en cada write al S3 (como metadata, o como parte del filename, o via conditional write con Version-ID). S3 (o un proxy) valida: si el TOKEN de la request es MENOR que el último TOKEN visto para ese lock, RECHAZA la operación. Worker A despierta con token 42, intenta write, S3 ya vio token 43 de worker B → rechazo. No corruption.
options.why: Correcto. Fencing tokens son el mecanismo canónico. La clave es que el RECURSO destino (S3 o proxy) valida el token, no confía en el 'estado del lock'. Even si worker A cree tener el lock, S3 sabe qué token fue el último autorizado y rechaza operaciones con token stale. Sin cooperación del recurso, no hay seguridad — solo esperanza. En S3 puro (sin conditional put by version-id + versioning), fencing tokens tradicionales no aplican directamente; requiere wrapper/proxy que valide, o app-level naming con token en filename.

options.text: Fencing tokens son parte de ZK — automáticamente resuelven todo.
options.why: ZK EXPONE el fencing token (zxid) pero no puede FORZAR al recurso destino a validarlo. La corrección requires cooperation. Muchos recursos (S3 puro, Redis SETs, etc.) no tienen concept de fencing token nativo — necesitas layer adicional.

options.text: Redlock resuelve el problema con majority quorum de Redis instances.
options.why: Falso — Kleppmann demostró que Redlock NO resuelve el pause scenario. Redlock provides mutual exclusion under normal conditions pero falla bajo pauses / clock jumps. Y no expone fencing token.

options.text: Simplemente usar shorter TTL en el lock.
options.why: Reduce probabilidad pero no elimina. Además shorter TTL causa más spurious lease expiration bajo variability normal. No resuelve el problema fundamental.

questions.explanation: Fencing tokens: monotonically increasing number generated per lock acquisition. Guarantees ordering. Usage: (1) Lock service (ZK, etcd) generates token on lock acquire. (2) Client includes token in every operation on the protected resource. (3) Resource validates: rejects operations with token < last seen. Requires resource support: (a) Database with conditional update on version — WHERE version = token AND version_lock <= token. (b) Custom middleware validating token. (c) Storage with conditional write (S3 conditional puts, DynamoDB conditional updates). (d) Application-level enforcement (worker validates before critical section, though race exists). Google Chubby's sequencer numbers are fencing tokens. Kafka leader epoch fencing prevents old leaders committing after election. HDFS write leases include epoch. Without fencing tokens, distributed locks are 'best effort' — good luck. The Kleppmann distinction: 'distributed lock without fencing token is not really a lock; it's a hint'.
questions.realWorld: Chubby's paper explicitly describes fencing sequencers. Kafka added leader epoch (KAFKA-1211) to prevent split-brain writes from zombie leaders. HDFS uses lease epoch. Etcd revision numbers can serve as fencing tokens. S3 conditional writes with version ID enable app-level fencing. Real bug: Cloudflare 2020 outage involved leader assumption without proper fencing.

references.title: Martin Kleppmann — 'How to do distributed locking'
Google Chubby paper — sequencer numbers section

questions.scenario: Raft cluster de 5 nodos sufre network flapping (partitions intermittentes de 200ms). Sistema entra en 'election storm': constantes leader elections, no progresa work. CPU al 100% en elections. Availability tanks.
questions.question: ¿Qué mecanismos previenen election storms?

options.text: Pre-Vote optimization: antes de incrementar term y comenzar election, candidate hace 'pre-vote' preguntando a peers 'me votarían?'. Si no obtiene mayoría de yes-hipotéticos, no incrementa term (evita disrupcionar leadership vigente). Ongaro Raft thesis lo describe.
options.why: Correcto. Pre-Vote (Ongaro thesis Section 9.6) previene 'disruptive server' — nodo particionado incrementaría term repetidamente, forzando new leader cada vez que reconecta. Con pre-vote, chequea primero si tendría chance real antes de disrupt. Etcd, Consul, tikv implementan pre-vote.

options.text: Randomized election timeouts (Raft default): cada nodo waits random duration antes de start election (ej. 150-300ms), evitando split votes cuando múltiples candidates lanzan simultáneamente.
options.why: Correcto. Es parte del diseño básico de Raft — evita split vote scenarios donde 3 nodos simultáneamente self-vote no obtiene mayoría. Randomization garantiza probabilísticamente que alguien lance primero. Sin esto, elections podrían fallar repetidamente.

options.text: Leader stickiness: leaders con lease no cede leadership solo por perder heartbeat brevemente — requiere quorum de followers confirmando need for election.
options.why: Correcto. Leader lease + grace periods evitan spurious elections por transient network hiccups. Some implementations (etcd) usan additional 'CheckQuorum' — leader periodically confirms it still has quorum contact; else step down.

options.text: Aumentar el timeout de elección a 30 segundos.
options.why: Mitiga pero causa slow detection genuine failures. Trade-off pobre. Preferable soluciones estructurales (pre-vote, quorum check) sobre timeout tuning.

options.text: Disable consensus y usar simple heartbeat.
options.why: Elimina safety del consensus — vuelve a split-brain territory. La solución no es abandonar consensus, es tunearlo correctly.

questions.explanation: Election storms happen when: (1) network flapping causes leader detection alternating; (2) split votes never resolve; (3) 'disruptive' followers reconnecting increment terms forcing re-election. Solutions: (1) Pre-Vote (Raft thesis Section 9.6) — check for votes hypothetically before incrementing term. Prevents disruptive node scenario. Adopted in etcd, TiKV. (2) Randomized election timeouts — Raft default (typically 150-300ms randomized). Prevents split votes. (3) Leader lease with CheckQuorum — leader steps down if loses quorum contact; prevents ancient leader disrupting. (4) Priority-based candidacy (some implementations) — preferred candidates try first, others wait. (5) Bounded terms — cap term jumps to prevent runaway increments. Real-world: network flapping en cloud (transient AZ issues, DNS blips) es common. Well-tuned Raft handles it; poorly tuned enters storms. Monitor election frequency as SLI.
questions.realWorld: Etcd 2015 had election storm bug fixed by Pre-Vote (issue etcd#3866). Consul similar improvements. TiKV explicitly documents pre-vote enabled. Sin these mechanisms, cluster puede quedar unavailable durante network chaos incluso cuando quorum de nodes están reachable — bad tuning issue.

references.title: Ongaro Raft thesis — Section 9.6 'Preventing disruptions when a server rejoins'

questions.scenario: Junior confuses coordination service (Zookeeper) con database. Piensa que puede almacenar user data en Zookeeper zNodes.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el uso APROPIADO de coordination services vs bases de datos?

options.text: Coordination services (ZK, etcd, Consul) están diseñados para SMALL amounts of critical metadata con strong consistency: config, service discovery, leader election, distributed locks, feature flags. Cada write requiere consensus (paga latencia). Storage total típicamente <100 MB. NO usarlos como database general purpose (millones de records, high write throughput) — el consensus overhead los hace lentos y caros.
options.why: Correcto. Coordination services optimizados para: (a) tamaño limitado (bytes/MB, no GB), (b) high consistency (linearizable reads/writes), (c) baja frecuencia de writes (~ hundreds/s no thousands), (d) alto valor por operación (critical metadata). Usar como DB regular es antipatrón: latencia alta (consensus RTT ~ms even in same DC), no soporta queries complex, expiring TTL primitives specific to coordination use cases. ZK docs explícitamente advisen contra almacenar > few MB. Etcd tiene 8GB soft limit.

options.text: Zookeeper puede ser tu database — es más consistente que Postgres.
options.why: Fatal misconception. Consistency doesn't equal general-purpose. ZK stores everything in memory (limited size), each write consensus'd (slow), no query language, single writer. Postgres/MySQL están optimizados para storage, queries, throughput muy diferentes.

options.text: Etcd/ZK escalan a cualquier tamaño de data.
options.why: Falso. Etcd tiene default 2GB backend limit (extensible a 8GB con caveats). Cada write consenso'd — throughput topa en single-thread consensus (typically ~10-50k writes/s in ideal conditions). Diseñado para metadata, no bulk data.

options.text: Consul es una DB moderna con service discovery bonus.
options.why: Consul KV tiene mismas limitations. La primary function es coordination + service catalog. Not designed as OLTP DB replacement.

questions.explanation: Coordination services vs databases: (1) Coordination — small metadata, strong consistency (linearizable), consensus per write (slow), low throughput (~10k writes/s), memory-resident (limited size). Use cases: leader election, service discovery, config, distributed locks, feature flags, membership. Examples: ZK, etcd, Consul, Chubby. (2) Databases — large data (TB), tunable consistency, high throughput (100k+ writes/s), disk-resident, complex queries. Postgres, MySQL, DynamoDB, Cassandra. Confusion arises because coordination services expose KV APIs similar to KV DBs. Key difference: coordination services trade throughput/size for STRONG consistency and specialized primitives (leases, watches, ephemeral nodes). Rule of thumb: if your data fits in RAM and needs consensus per operation, coordination service. If large, high-throughput, and can tolerate eventual, DB. Con Kubernetes (heavy etcd user), typical control plane etcd size < 1GB even for large clusters. Metadata pattern, not bulk data.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes etcd stores cluster state (nodes, pods, configs) — typically <1GB for large clusters. If you tried to store user data or logs in it, would collapse. Kafka uses ZK (deprecated for KRaft) for broker metadata, controller election — not for message data (that's the log files). Consul KV stores config + service catalog. Chubby paper explícitamente 'small pieces of critical data'.

questions.scenario: Cluster de 10.000 nodos (Consul, Cassandra) necesita saber qué nodos están vivos. Consensus (Raft) no escala a 10.000 miembros. ¿Qué mecanismo alternativo?
questions.question: ¿Qué protocolo se usa para membership eficiente a gran escala?

options.text: SWIM (Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Membership) — gossip protocol donde nodos periódicamente 'ping' random peers, propagando membership changes via gossip. Falla detection en O(log N) latency, network overhead O(1) por nodo. Consul, HashiCorp Serf, Cassandra usan SWIM o variants.
options.why: Correcto. SWIM (Das-Gupta-Motivala 2002) es el gossip protocol standard para large-scale membership. Properties: (1) O(1) network cost per node (fixed messages/period regardless of cluster size). (2) O(log N) latency para propagate membership change. (3) Suspicion mechanism (mark suspicious before failed) reduces false positives. (4) Eventual consistency de membership (no total order needed). Ideal para 10k+ nodes donde consensus is impractical. Serf, Consul, Cassandra, Riak use variants.

options.text: Raft con 10.000 miembros.
options.why: Impractical: Raft leader must contact quorum (5001) each operation. Latency + bandwidth explode. Raft designed for <10 nodes typical, max <100 (con optimizations). 10k nodes es fuera de scope.

options.text: Centralized health checker que pings todos los nodos.
options.why: SPOF. Además ping 10k nodes serially es lento; parallel es massive load. Bandwidth from central health checker ~ N. Doesn't scale.

options.text: TCP keepalive.
options.why: TCP keepalive is peer-to-peer (each connection). No gives cluster-wide membership view. Wrong abstraction level.

questions.explanation: Membership at scale: (1) Consensus (Raft, Paxos) — strong consistency but doesn't scale beyond ~10 nodes. Good for coordination services with small membership. (2) Gossip protocols (SWIM, HyParView) — weak consistency, eventual, scale to thousands. Trade consistency for scalability. (3) Central heartbeat — SPOF, doesn't scale. SWIM details: (a) Each node periodically PINGs a random peer. (b) If no ack, indirect ping via other peers (before declaring dead). (c) Membership changes gossip'd piggyback on pings. (d) Suspicion phase: 'suspicious' node marked, revoked if it responds; else 'failed' after timeout. Reduces false positives dramatically. Complexity: O(1) per node per period regardless of N. Failure detection latency: O(log N) periods. Variants: SWIM+ (Lifeguard), HyParView. Some implementations combine consensus for critical membership decisions (leader election) with gossip for scale (membership discovery). Kafka doesn't use gossip (Kafka is limited scale ~thousands brokers max, uses controller). Cassandra uses gossip heavily. Consul combines Raft (for a few 'servers') with SWIM (for many 'clients').
questions.realWorld: Consul architecture separates Consul Servers (Raft, ~3-5) from Consul Agents (SWIM, potentially 10k+). Cassandra uses gossip for membership + Merkle trees for anti-entropy. HashiCorp Serf is standalone SWIM library. Uber Ringpop uses SWIM. Kubernetes uses etcd (Raft) for master state, kubelet heartbeats for node health (centralized-ish but scoped).

references.title: Das, Gupta, Motivala — 'SWIM: Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Process Group Membership Protocol', DSN 2002

questions.scenario: Google Spanner ofrece 'external consistency' global (mismo garantía que serializable + linearizable) across data centers globally. ¿Cómo lo logra sin latencia prohibitiva?
questions.question: ¿Qué innovación clave hace posible Spanner?

options.text: Software-only Paxos across DCs.
options.why: Insuficiente — solo Paxos across DCs paga round-trip inter-DC latency (~10-100ms) por cada transaction. Otras sistemas también hacen Paxos across DCs. La innovación de Spanner es ADEMÁS de Paxos, algo más.

options.text: TrueTime API: Google datacenters equipados con GPS receivers y atomic clocks. TrueTime.now() devuelve intervalo [earliest, latest] con incertidumbre bounded (~7ms típicamente). Spanner uses 'commit wait' — after acquiring locks and choosing timestamp, wait until TrueTime.after(commit_timestamp) confirms real time passed the timestamp. Esto garantiza que transactions commit'ed antes en real-time no vean timestamps posteriores. Con TrueTime tight bounds, commit wait es short (~7ms).
options.why: Correcto. TrueTime es la innovación técnica clave (Corbett et al. OSDI 2012). Sin TrueTime, external consistency global requeriría coordinación cross-DC per read (latencia prohibitiva). Con TrueTime, each Spanner replica has bounded clock uncertainty. Transaction commit waits out the uncertainty (typically 7ms) — after wait, guarantees timestamp is in past. Reads at timestamp T see all commits < T without cross-DC coordination. Enabler: physical hardware (GPS + atomic clocks in each DC), managed by TimeMaster processes. AWS TimeSync provides similar sub-ms sync.

options.text: Spanner NO ofrece linearizabilidad global — solo eventual consistency across regions.
options.why: Falso. Spanner explícitamente offers 'external consistency' which is strict serializability (linearizable + serializable) GLOBALLY. Es el whole point del sistema. Paper de 2012 lo demuestra formalmente.

options.text: Usa vector clocks a escala planetaria.
options.why: Vector clocks capturan causalidad pero no orden real-time. Además scaling vector clocks a millions of nodes es impractical. Spanner uses TrueTime specifically porque vector clocks NO son sufficient para external consistency.

questions.explanation: Spanner (Corbett et al. OSDI 2012) is one of the most influential distributed systems papers. Innovation: physical clock synchronization within bounded uncertainty enables efficient linearizability at global scale. Architecture: (1) Data partitioned into ranges, each replicated via Paxos across zones. (2) Two-phase commit for cross-shard transactions. (3) TrueTime provides bounded clock uncertainty via GPS + atomic clocks. (4) Commit wait: after choosing timestamp T and getting Paxos consensus, wait until TrueTime.now().earliest > T. This ensures T is definitely in the past. (5) Reads at timestamp T can proceed at any replica without coordination (using TrueTime to ensure freshness). Consequences: (a) Writes pay ~7ms commit wait (uncertainty window). (b) Reads are efficient (no cross-DC coordination for timestamp'd reads). (c) External consistency (strict serializability) with global scope. Impact: showed physical clock sync at scale is possible; inspired CockroachDB (HLC without GPS, less strict), YugabyteDB, AWS Aurora, TiDB (approximate approaches). AWS TimeSync (2017) provides GPS-backed sub-ms clock sync in EC2 enabling similar approaches.
questions.realWorld: Google Spanner backs Ads, Play, Gmail. AWS TimeSync provides ~1ms uncertainty (advertising 'microsecond precision' in some regions). CockroachDB uses Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) with bounded uncertainty (NTP-based, wider). FoundationDB uses different approach (deterministic simulation testing). YugabyteDB claims Spanner-like external consistency. Sin TrueTime-class clock sync, linearizability global requires cross-DC coordination per operation — impossibly slow.

references.title: Corbett et al. — 'Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database', OSDI 2012

questions.scenario: Team propone Two-Phase Commit (2PC) para coordinar writes across 3 microservicios (Order, Inventory, Payment). Otro senior lo desaconseja fuertemente.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son los problemas fundamentales de 2PC?

options.text: Bloqueante: en fase 2 (commit/abort), si el coordinator falla después de que participants prepararon (locked resources), participants quedan en 'in-doubt' state — locks retenidos indefinidamente hasta que coordinator resuelva. Puede tumbar el sistema.
options.why: Correcto. 2PC blocking problem is fundamental. Después del PREPARE, participants adquieren locks + persisten log 'ready to commit'. Si coordinator crashes antes del COMMIT/ABORT message, participants no saben qué hacer — locks retenidos, otros writes bloqueados. Requiere manual intervention o wait for coordinator recovery. Es por esto que 2PC no se usa across services en producción moderna.

options.text: SPOF del coordinator: si el coordinator es único, su caída bloquea el sistema. 3PC intenta resolver pero introduce otros problemas y no funciona bajo network partitions.
options.why: Correcto. Coordinator es central para decision. Sin él, decision no puede tomarse. 3PC (Three-Phase Commit, Skeen 1982) intenta adding pre-commit phase to reduce blocking, pero no es safe under network partitions (proved). 3PC nunca ganó adopción por complexity + limitations.

options.text: No funciona con REST/HTTP/message queues — requiere XA transactions o similar coordination protocol soportado por cada participant.
options.why: Correcto. 2PC requires participants implementen XA (X/Open Distributed Transaction Processing) o similar. Kafka NO es XA-compatible. HTTP is stateless. Most modern databases don't advertise XA (o lo advertise pero con caveats). Cross-service 2PC via REST es impractical. Es porque saga/orchestration reemplazaron 2PC en distributed systems modernos.

options.text: Performance: cada transaction paga 2 round-trips (prepare + commit) + persistence en cada participant. Latency ~2x normal transaction.
options.why: Correcto. 2PC pays 2 round-trips minimum + persistent log writes at prepare (durable) + commit. Vs single-phase local commit, es varias veces slower. Throughput limitado. Solo justificable si la atomicity es worth the cost, y hoy sagas/orchestration ofrecen alternatives con better trade-offs.

options.text: 2PC es el standard moderno; Saga es solo para sistemas legacy.
options.why: Invertido. 2PC es el approach 'classical' (1970s-80s theory). Modern distributed systems (microservicios, event-driven) usan sagas / eventual consistency + compensations precisamente porque 2PC no funciona bien across services.

questions.explanation: 2PC (Two-Phase Commit, Gray-Lamport 1970s): (1) PREPARE phase — coordinator asks all participants 'ready?'. Each acquires locks + writes 'prepared' to log + votes YES/NO. (2) COMMIT phase — if all YES, coordinator sends COMMIT; else ABORT. Participants commit/abort locally. Problems: (1) Blocking on coordinator failure post-prepare. (2) SPOF coordinator. (3) Requires participant cooperation (XA support). (4) 2x round-trip latency. (5) Doesn't work across message queues or non-XA systems. Alternativas modernas: (1) Sagas — sequence of local transactions with compensations. Eventual consistency but scales. Recovery via saga log or orchestrator. (2) Outbox pattern — event published atomically with local write. Downstream reacts eventually. (3) Choreography vs orchestration for saga coordination (Temporal, Cadence, Step Functions). Some systems still use 2PC internally: XA transactions between same-vendor DB instances (Oracle, MSSQL), Kafka Streams transactions (2PC-like within Kafka). Cross-vendor / cross-service, sagas dominant. Rule: prefer designing for eventual consistency + compensation over 2PC.
questions.realWorld: Google Spanner uses 2PC internally combined with Paxos (2PC across Paxos groups for cross-shard tx). Isolated in one system Spanner is production. Cross-service 2PC via distributed transaction managers (Tuxedo, MTS) has largely been replaced by sagas in microservicios era. Booking.com, Uber, Airbnb all use sagas for cross-service coordination. Chris Richardson's 'Microservices Patterns' extensively covers why sagas over 2PC.

questions.scenario: Sistema distribuido necesita ordenar events. Options: (a) wall-clock timestamp, (b) Lamport clock, (c) vector clock, (d) sequencer central (auto-increment global).
questions.question: ¿Cuál usa qué y por qué?

options.text: Wall-clock: siempre correcto, es la referencia natural del tiempo.
options.why: Falso. Wall-clock drift/skew entre nodes, NTP jumps, VM pausas. Usar wall-clock para ordering distribuido causa bugs sutiles (ver Cassandra LWW issues). Solo útil si tienes GPS + atomic clocks o TrueTime-like.

options.text: Cada uno tiene su nicho: Wall-clock — OK cuando bounded clock skew (TrueTime, TimeSync). Lamport clock — orden total lógico consistente con causalidad, pero NO distingue concurrentes. Vector clock — captura orden parcial + detecta concurrency, pero metadata O(N nodes). Central sequencer — orden total simple, pero SPOF y bottleneck.
options.why: Correcto y matizado. Cada mecanismo tiene use case: (1) Wall-clock con bounded uncertainty (Spanner TrueTime, HLC) — orden real-time + escala. (2) Lamport clock (1978) — logical timestamps consistent con happens-before, O(1) metadata, provides total order (con tie-breaking) pero no distingue concurrency. (3) Vector clocks — detect concurrency (writes concurrent son incomparables), pero O(N) metadata (N nodes), no scale to millions. (4) Central sequencer (Kafka partition offsets, DynamoDB stream sequence) — simple total order per partition, but limited scale (single writer). (5) HLC (Hybrid Logical Clocks, Kulkarni 2014) — combines wall-clock + logical, adopted in CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, MongoDB 3.6+.

options.text: Vector clocks son siempre superiores.
options.why: Falso. Vector clocks pagan O(N) metadata per event. Con miles de writers, prohibitivo. Compact representations (dotted vector versions) mitigan pero no eliminan. Trade-off, no dominance.

options.text: Central sequencer siempre — más simple.
options.why: SPOF + bottleneck. Kafka partition sequences funcionan solo dentro de partition. Global central sequencer no escala. Elegir según requirements.

questions.explanation: Ordering en distributed systems tiene rich taxonomy: (1) Wall-clock: physical time, simple but drift-prone. Only trust con GPS/atomic sync (Spanner). (2) Lamport clocks (1978): logical counter, increment on send + max on receive. Consistent with happens-before (a→b => L(a)<L(b)) but converse doesn't hold. Total order requires tie-breaking (node ID). (3) Vector clocks (Fidge/Mattern 1988): vector [n1:v1, n2:v2...]. Fully captures happens-before + detects concurrency. But O(N) metadata. (4) Version vectors: variant for versioning data replicas. (5) Interval Tree Clocks (Almeida 2008): dynamic membership, more efficient. (6) Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC, Kulkarni 2014): combines physical + logical. Small metadata (int64), bounded uncertainty from wall-clock, causality-consistent. Adopted by CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, MongoDB. (7) Central sequencer: monotonic auto-increment. Simple, total order, but scale-limited. Kafka partition offset is bounded (per-partition). Elección: trade-offs vary. Modern trend: HLC as best-all-around for distributed DBs.
questions.realWorld: Cassandra uses microsecond wall-clock timestamps (LWW), susceptible to drift issues (Jepsen tests demonstrated). Dynamo used vector clocks originally, moved to LWW for simplicity. CockroachDB uses HLC. Spanner uses TrueTime. Kafka partition offsets are per-partition central sequencers. Bitcoin uses Merkle DAG (partial ordering via hash-based). Understanding which ordering mechanism your system uses is key to debugging distributed anomalies.

references.title: Lamport — 'Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events'

questions.scenario: Necesitas que múltiples servicios reciban notificación cuando config cambia en etcd (feature flag toggle, service registration). No quieres polling.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el mecanismo apropiado?

options.text: Watch API: etcd/ZK/Consul exponen 'watch' — client subscribe a un key/prefix, coordination service push notification cuando value changes. Long-lived connection (gRPC stream en etcd, TCP en ZK). Escalable: order of magnitude cheaper que polling. Idempotent y con revision numbers para recuperar from any point.
options.why: Correcto. Watch es primitive fundamental de coordination services. etcd exposes gRPC watch stream — client subscribes to key/prefix + start revision; server pushes events (PUT, DELETE) as they happen. Efficient para thousands de watchers per key. ZK usa 'watches' (one-shot, must re-register — más pesado). Consul usa 'blocking queries' (long-polling). Kubernetes controller pattern relies heavily on etcd watches — every controller watches its resource types.

options.text: Polling cada 1 segundo.
options.why: Ineficiente y con latency of at least 1s per change. Con N clients polling M keys → N*M requests/s carga. Además detects stale changes minutes after they happen if poll interval large. Watch is order-of-magnitude better.

options.text: Publish-subscribe via Kafka.
options.why: Válido pero introduce Kafka as dependency + coordination between systems (etcd config → publish to Kafka → consumers). Complejo cuando el mismo coordination service ya expone watch.

options.text: Cada servicio se conecta directamente a la app que hace el cambio para notificarse.
options.why: N-to-N coupling nightmare. La app que muta config tendría que conocer todos los consumers. Coordination service es exactamente el intermediary para desacoplarlos.

questions.explanation: Watch mechanisms are essential primitives in coordination services: (1) etcd watch: gRPC streaming, watch by key or prefix, from any revision (allows recovery from disconnect without missing events). Server pushes events. (2) ZK watches: one-shot (must re-register after each event, more overhead), tied to session. (3) Consul blocking queries: HTTP long-polling — client sends query with 'wait' param + 'index' from previous response; server holds until change or timeout. HTTP-friendly but less efficient than gRPC streams. (4) Kafka: not really 'watch' — consumer group polls topic. Usage patterns: (a) Kubernetes controllers watch resource kinds, reconcile on change. (b) Service discovery: services watch service registry, update local caches. (c) Feature flags: apps watch flag keys, update behavior in real-time. (d) Configuration: apps watch config, hot-reload. Considerations: (a) Watch scaling — thousands of watchers per key increases server load; etcd/ZK have limits. (b) Watch recovery — if connection breaks, client should resume from last known revision to avoid missing events. (c) Watch storms — many watchers reacting to a change can cause thundering herd downstream.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes uses etcd watches pervasively — kube-controller-manager watches deployments/pods/services. CoreDNS watches services. Envoy sidecar watches xDS APIs (control plane push config changes). Consul-template watches Consul KV/services to regenerate config files. Sin watch primitives, sistemas serían polling-heavy y less responsive.

questions.scenario: Raft cluster de 5 nodos. Necesitas añadir 2 nuevos nodos (para escalar a 7). Preocupas por safety durante la transición.
questions.question: ¿Cómo se hace safely membership change en Raft?

options.text: Añadir todos los nodos simultáneamente — más rápido.
options.why: PELIGROSO. Cambiar quorum de 3-of-5 a 4-of-7 simultaneously puede crear dos quorums disjuntos temporalmente (leaders elegidos por old y new configurations concurrentemente). Raft prohíbe explicitly este cambio directo.

options.text: Joint consensus (Raft original): configuration change goes through intermediate 'joint' state where BOTH old and new majorities are required to commit. Fase intermedia dura mientras el cambio propagates. Safe: durante transition, decisions require agreement from both quorums, preventing disjoint decisions.
options.why: Correcto para Raft original (Ongaro thesis). Joint consensus: log entry 'change to config Cnew' committed only when majorities of BOTH Cold and Cnew agree. Once committed, new configuration takes effect. Prevents split-brain during transition. Alternative simpler mechanism 'single-server changes' (add/remove one at a time) also supported — safe if change one node at a time.

options.text: Tumbar el cluster, reconfigure, restart.
options.why: Downtime innecesario cuando Raft soporta live membership changes. Además si el restart falla o hay bugs, pierdes state. Live reconfig es más safe.

options.text: Añadir nodos como 'observers' que no votan.
options.why: Es UNA técnica válida (etcd 'learner nodes') pero no responde al problema. Learners son un stepping stone (recibir data primero, luego promote a voter una vez sincronizados) — el add-to-voter step aún requiere safe reconfig.

questions.explanation: Raft cluster membership changes fundamentales para production ops. Techniques: (1) Joint consensus (Raft thesis Section 4): transitional Cold,new config requiring both majorities. Safe but complex. (2) Single-server changes: add or remove one at a time. Simpler — Raft can prove safety con single change at a time (quorums overlap by design). Etcd, Consul use this. (3) Learner nodes (etcd 'learners'): new nodes join as non-voting learners first, catch up on log without affecting quorum, then promoted to voters. Prevents adding un-caught-up node that would slow quorum. Similar in TiKV, CockroachDB. Considerations: (a) Data catchup — new node must snapshot + tail log before contributing. If gap huge, catchup takes long. (b) Timing — during transition, cluster tolerance may temporarily reduce (adding 1 to 3→4 nodes: still tolerates 1 during transition but Cnew tolerates 1 vs Cold tolerates 1, be careful). (c) Automation — production changes should be operator-managed with monitoring, not batch scripts. Etcd/Consul tooling for this. Sin safe membership change, ops de cluster resize would require downtime.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes control plane etcd routinely resized (add nodes for HA, remove degraded). Uses etcd's single-server change or learner mode. CockroachDB decommissioning uses safe range rebalancing before removing node. Consul cluster ops similar. Bugs en membership changes (rare) have caused split-brain — Kleppmann and Aphyr have documented cases. Always follow docs y test in non-prod first.

references.title: Ongaro Raft thesis — Ch. 4 Cluster membership changes

questions.scenario: Etcd cluster serves Kubernetes API. Read load es 100x write load (API server queries pods, services frequently). Reads through Raft leader hit CPU limit.
questions.question: ¿Qué opciones existen para escalar reads en un sistema consensus?

options.text: Serializable reads locally en any follower: skip Raft, read local state directly. Fast pero puede ser stale.
options.why: Reduce loads pero pierdes linearizability. Follower puede tener stale data (missed recent commits). Aceptable for eventual reads pero no for strong reads necessary in Kubernetes (leader lease read violaría if enabled).

options.text: Read from any follower with 'read lease' or 'readIndex' optimization: leader confirms it's still leader (heartbeat quorum) + follower waits until its log reaches leader's commitIndex. Linearizable but avoids leader routing. Alternative: 'lease read' — leader with valid lease can serve reads without quorum check (assuming clock sync).
options.why: Correcto. Raft 'ReadIndex' optimization (Ongaro thesis Section 6.4): (1) Leader confirma current leadership via heartbeat exchange with quorum. (2) Leader records commitIndex at that moment. (3) Follower serves read once its log reaches that index. Linearizable + avoids full quorum. Lease-based read: leader with valid lease serves reads without quorum check (assumes bounded clock skew, no other leader could exist within lease). Etcd supports both. Enable read scaling significantly.

options.text: Añadir más nodos al cluster para más follower capacity.
options.why: Añadir nodos INCREMENTA write latency (larger quorum). Y default without ReadIndex/lease, reads still go through leader. Additional nodes need to serve reads via readIndex mechanism.

options.text: Replicar toda la data a memcached delante.
options.why: Anti-patrón: Kubernetes state must be linearizable (leader election, resource versioning). Cache stale data breaks Kubernetes semantics. Coordination service data no debería cachearse ingenuously.

questions.explanation: Read scaling en Raft: default reads via leader (leader can serve or need quorum for linearizable read). Optimizations: (1) ReadIndex: cheaper way to serve linearizable reads. Leader heartbeats quorum to confirm leadership, records commitIndex. Follower can serve read once its state includes that commitIndex. Reduces leader load. (2) Lease-based read: leader with valid lease serves reads without any coordination (fastest). Requires clock sync assumption. Preferred in etcd, CockroachDB. Safety: lease must be shorter than election timeout to prevent zombie leader serving. (3) Learner nodes: non-voting followers that can serve stale reads. Explicit tradeoff for eventual reads. (4) Consistent reads via reading committed prefix: for use cases tolerating slight staleness. Kubernetes API tolerates versioned reads (resourceVersion parameter). Real balance: writes require Raft consensus (always); reads can scale via ReadIndex/lease. Etcd 3.x has readIndex enabled by default. Learners for scale-out reads (added in etcd 3.4).
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes at scale (10k+ nodes) hits etcd read limits. Solutions: (1) etcd learners for scaled reads, (2) API server watch cache (reduces etcd load), (3) etcd version upgrade to 3.4+ with learner support. TiKV serves reads from Raft leader with lease optimization. CockroachDB uses similar. Zoom, Cloudflare etc. face this in high-throughput deployments. Sin these optimizations, Raft leader is bottleneck.

references.title: Ongaro Raft thesis — Section 6.4 'Processing read-only queries more efficiently'

questions.scenario: Necesitas HA global across 3 AWS regions (us-east, eu-west, ap-south) usando Raft. Cada region tiene 1 nodo (3 total). Latency inter-region: 80-200ms.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son los trade-offs y consideraciones?

options.text: Trade-offs: (1) Write latency = max(RTT to majority) = ~80-200ms per write (paga inter-region roundtrip). (2) Tolerates 1 region failure. (3) Leader in one region → clients in other regions pay cross-region RTT for writes. (4) Learners in additional regions para stale reads locally. (5) Alternativas: partition data per region (data locality), or use different consistency (multi-master eventual for latency, sacrificing strong). Design decision depends on tolerable write latency, data locality patterns.
options.why: Correcto y matizado. Global Raft is possible pero SLOW. Write latency dominated por WAN RTT to majority. Con 3 regions (us-east/eu-west/ap-south), quorum requires 2 regions, so writer pays ~100ms roundtrip minimum. Alternatives: (a) Regional partitioning — datos ubicados en region más relevante, cross-region only for global reads. Spanner does this per range. (b) Multi-region with follower reads — reads local, writes global. (c) Multi-master eventual (Cassandra, DynamoDB Global Tables) — writes local, reads local, sacrifice strong consistency. Elección depende de business requirements.

options.text: Global Raft es siempre mejor porque garantiza strong consistency.
options.why: Ignora costo de latency. Strong consistency global paga ~100ms+ per write minimum. Muchos use cases prefer local writes con eventual global sync (sacrificing linearizability for latency). Depend on requirements.

options.text: Multi-master eventual siempre es mejor por latency.
options.why: Ignora need de strong consistency para algunos data (financial, invariantes). Multi-master eventual sacrifices consistency — write conflicts inevitable. Depend on use case.

options.text: 5 nodos por region para más HA.
options.why: Malinterpreta: quorum is global across all nodes, not per-region. Adding nodes per region doesn't help if quorum requires cross-region. Añade cost sin beneficio primary.

questions.explanation: Multi-region consensus is genuinely hard — physics (light speed) sets latency floor. Trade-offs: (1) Global Raft/Paxos with quorum across regions — writes pay WAN RTT. Consistency guaranteed. Availability: tolerates 1 region loss (with 3 regions, majority 2 needed). Google Spanner does this at planetary scale con TrueTime optimizing. (2) Regional partitioning — data assigned to region closest to users. Cross-region access via async replication or on-demand. Spanner's ranges assigned to zones. CockroachDB regional tables. (3) Multi-master eventual — Cassandra, DynamoDB Global Tables. Writes local latency, reads local latency, conflict resolution eventual (LWW or CRDT). Sacrifices strong consistency. (4) Hierarchical — regional strong + global eventual (Kafka MirrorMaker style). Considerations: (a) Data locality patterns — how much data is truly global vs regional? (b) Compliance — GDPR requires EU data stay in EU. Regional Raft satisfies. (c) Failover complexity — losing a region should not require manual intervention (auto-failover via consensus). Modern DBs (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB) offer multi-region with fine-grained control per table/row.
questions.realWorld: Google Spanner: global consensus with TrueTime, backing Ads, Play. AWS DynamoDB Global Tables: multi-master eventual (~1s replication). CockroachDB Multi-Region: strong consistency with 'survive region failure' declaration per table. YugabyteDB similar. Kubernetes federations (KubeFed) are eventual multi-region. Netflix multi-region Cassandra: eventual, apps designed for it.

questions.scenario: Startup pregunta si Raft es 'always available'. Ingeniero explica que Raft trade availability por consistency.
questions.question: ¿En qué escenarios Raft cluster deja de estar available y por qué?

options.text: Cuando pierdes quorum (más de F nodos caídos con N=2F+1), cluster cannot commit writes ni serve linearizable reads. Choose safety (no writes) over risking inconsistency. Ejemplos: (1) 3-node cluster, 2 down → cannot commit. (2) Split-brain partition where local side is minority → minority unavailable. Deliberadamente CP (in CAP terms): sacrifice availability in favor of consistency during partition/failure.
options.why: Correcto. Raft explícitamente elige C over A when P (partition/failure) — es un sistema CP. Losing quorum makes cluster unable to make forward progress: cannot elect leader (needs quorum votes), cannot commit writes (needs quorum acks), cannot serve linearizable reads. Aceptamos esta unavailability por safety — alternative (multi-master eventual, some AP systems) accepts inconsistency to stay available. Kubernetes en etcd quorum loss → control plane cannot progress (cannot schedule new pods) — matches Raft's design deliberately.

options.text: Raft es siempre available porque tiene N-1 tolerance.
options.why: Falso: N-1 nodos caídos = quorum lost. Tolerance is F = (N-1)/2. With N=3, tolerates 1. With N=5, tolerates 2. Not N-1.

options.text: Raft nunca es unavailable — solo latencies aumentan.
options.why: Confusión. Under quorum loss, Raft cluster is genuinely unavailable for writes/linearizable reads (not just slow — cannot make progress at all). Es design choice explicit.

options.text: Raft es más available que multi-master systems.
options.why: Inverso. Multi-master systems (Cassandra AP with local quorum) can accept writes on any partition side (sacrificing consistency for availability). Raft prevents writes on minority side (preserving consistency, sacrificing availability). Different trade-off.

questions.explanation: Raft (y consensus systems generally) sacrifice availability for consistency during failures/partitions. Availability requires quorum: (1) Write availability — needs quorum of nodes reachable AND up-to-date to commit. (2) Linearizable read availability — needs leader confirmed still leader (heartbeat quorum) via ReadIndex, or valid lease. (3) Serial stale read availability — any follower can serve. Failure scenarios: (a) Node crashes < F — cluster tolerates, quorum still available, no downtime. (b) Node crashes > F — quorum lost, cluster stuck. (c) Network partition — majority side operates, minority side unavailable. (d) Leader crash — new election (few seconds typical). Design consequence: Raft = CP en CAP. AP alternatives (Cassandra with consistency ONE): available even in minority partition but returns possibly stale/inconsistent data. Rule for design: use Raft-based (etcd, Consul) when correctness is paramount (Kubernetes control plane, service discovery). Use AP systems when availability paramount even under partition (analytics, dashboards, non-critical data).
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes cluster with etcd quorum loss: kubectl commands fail, new pods cannot be scheduled, existing pods continue running (kubelets have cached state). Recovery: restore quorum (majority nodes back), cluster resumes. Cassandra with consistency ONE writes always succeed but reads may be stale. Netflix chose EVCache (eventual) for many caches accepting AP. AWS DynamoDB default is eventual, ConsistentRead for strong. Choose CAP position deliberately per use case.

questions.scenario: Blockchain forums discuss 'Byzantine fault tolerance'. ¿Qué es y cuándo aplica?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la diferencia entre crash-only failures y Byzantine failures?

options.text: Crash-only (fail-stop) failures: nodo o funciona correctamente o se cae completamente (silent). Raft, Paxos asumen esto. Byzantine failures: nodo puede comportarse ARBITRARIAMENTE (malicious, buggy, corrupted) — enviar mensajes contradictorios a distintos peers, mentir sobre estado. Requiere protocols más costosos: PBFT, HotStuff, requieren N ≥ 3F+1 (vs 2F+1 crash). Necesario en trustless environments: blockchains, sistemas donde nodes son independientes (Bitcoin miners) o subject to attack. En intra-datacenter con nodes trusted, crash-only assumption es correcto y más barato.
options.why: Correcto. Crash faults: benign failure, node stops responding. Byzantine faults: any behavior including malicious, contradictory messages, corrupt data. Byzantine consensus (Lamport-Shostak-Pease 1982) requires more replicas (N=3F+1) y mechanisms como signed messages (avoiding equivocation). Practical: blockchains (Bitcoin PoW, Ethereum PoS, Tendermint BFT) need BFT because miners/validators are untrusted. Intra-datacenter systems (Kubernetes, database clusters) assume nodes are trustworthy (bugs happen but not maliciously) — crash-tolerance suffices. HotStuff (Facebook Libra) improved BFT efficiency. PBFT is classic reference.

options.text: Son lo mismo — nodo caído es nodo malicioso.
options.why: Fundamentalmente diferentes. Caído es SILENT (no responde); malicioso puede responder INCORRECTAMENTE (mensajes contradictorios, valores inválidos). Requerimientos de protocol y network cost diferentes.

options.text: Byzantine solo aplica a blockchain.
options.why: Blockchain is prime use case pero también aplica en cualquier trustless / multi-party systems: federated systems where different orgs run nodes, security-critical systems that could be compromised, cross-cloud federations.

options.text: PBFT ha reemplazado Raft.
options.why: No — Raft es dominant en trusted environments (más eficiente). PBFT y variants dominan en trustless environments. Ambos coexisten para distintos use cases.

questions.explanation: Failure models: (1) Crash-stop (fail-stop): node crashes and stays down. Simplest. Raft, Paxos. N=2F+1. (2) Crash-recovery: node may crash and later recover. Slight extension. (3) Omission: node may not send/receive some messages but doesn't lie. (4) Byzantine (arbitrary): node may behave anyhow — silence, wrong values, contradictory messages to different peers. Lamport-Shostak-Pease 1982 'Byzantine Generals'. Requires N=3F+1 with signed messages (or 3F+1 without signatures using more rounds). Protocols: (a) PBFT (Castro-Liskov 1999) — first practical Byzantine consensus, ~cubic message complexity in N. (b) HotStuff (2019) — linear message complexity, foundation of Diem/Libra. (c) Tendermint — BFT for blockchain (Cosmos). (d) Nakamoto consensus (Bitcoin) — probabilistic BFT via PoW. Cost comparison: Byzantine ~10x more messages than crash-only. Use Byzantine when: untrusted participants (blockchain, federated), high-value data with security paramount. Use crash-only in trusted environments (own datacenter, cloud with same account).
questions.realWorld: Bitcoin uses Nakamoto consensus (PoW). Ethereum 2.0 uses Casper (PoS BFT). Hyperledger Fabric uses variant BFT. Facebook Libra (paused) used HotStuff BFT. Zoom, Slack, Kubernetes: crash-only (trust their nodes). AWS DynamoDB internal replication: crash-only. Cross-org federations: could benefit from BFT (avoid single org corrupting). Design decision based on trust model.

references.title: Lamport, Shostak, Pease — 'The Byzantine Generals Problem', TOPLAS 1982
Castro, Liskov — 'Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance', OSDI 1999
